harmonic.definition: One of the pure sine waves stacked up to make a note. Harmonics sit at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, and their mix decides the tone.

frequency.definition: How many times a wave repeats each second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency sounds higher in pitch.

pitch.definition: How high or low a note sounds. It follows the frequency of the fundamental.

tone.definition: The character of a sound apart from its pitch or volume: bright, dull, buzzy, hollow. It comes mostly from the mix of harmonics.

fundamental.definition: The lowest and usually strongest harmonic in a note. Its frequency is the pitch you hear.

spectrum.definition: A picture of how much of each frequency is in a sound. Bright sounds have energy far to the right; dark sounds do not.

aliasing.definition: Harsh, out-of-tune whistles that appear when a digital sound contains frequencies too high to represent. It is most noticeable on high notes. Anti-aliasing is what prevents it.

cutoff.definition: The frequency where a filter starts to turn the sound down. Above it (for a low-pass) harmonics fade away.

resonance.definition: A boost at the cutoff frequency that adds a peak. High settings give a whistling, vocal edge and can make the filter ring.

low-pass.definition: A filter that lets low frequencies through and turns high ones down. It makes sound darker.

high-pass.definition: A filter that lets high frequencies through and turns low ones down. It makes sound thinner.

band-pass.definition: A filter that keeps a band of frequencies around the cutoff and turns down everything above and below. It sounds narrow, like a phone.

envelope.definition: A shape that changes over the life of one note: it starts when you press a key and finishes after you let go. It has attack, decay, sustain and release stages.

attack.definition: The time an envelope takes to rise from nothing to its peak after a key goes down.

decay.definition: The time an envelope takes to fall from its peak to the sustain level.

sustain.definition: The level an envelope holds while a key stays down. It is a level, not a time.

release.definition: The time an envelope takes to fall to nothing after you let go of the key.

velocity.definition: How hard you hit a key. Harder presses give higher velocity values, which can make notes louder or brighter.

lfo.definition: A low frequency oscillator: a wave too slow to hear as a note (0.01 to 50 Hz), used to move other controls up and down automatically.

modulation.definition: One control changing another over time. A source (such as an LFO) moves a destination (such as cutoff) by an amount.

vibrato.definition: A gentle, regular wobble in pitch. You get it by sending a slow LFO to pitch.

detune.definition: Setting two oscillators very slightly apart in pitch. The small difference makes a slow, shimmering beat that thickens the sound.

cents.definition: A tiny pitch unit: 100 cents make one semitone, and 1,200 make an octave.

semitone.definition: The smallest step on a piano, from one key to the next. Twelve semitones make an octave.

octave.definition: A doubling of frequency. Notes an octave apart sound like the same note, higher or lower.

pulse-width.definition: On a pulse wave, the share of each cycle spent high. 50% is a hollow square wave; narrower settings sound thinner and nasal.

white-noise.definition: Random hiss with equal energy at every frequency, so it sounds bright, like static.

pink-noise.definition: Random hiss with less energy in the highs than white noise, so it sounds softer, like rain or a waterfall.

gate.definition: The on/off signal from the keyboard: on while a key is down, off when you let go. Envelopes start from it.

polyphony.definition: The ability to play several notes at once. Each note uses one voice.

mono.definition: A mode where only one note plays at a time. A new key replaces the old one.

legato.definition: Playing notes joined together. In Legato mode, a note played while another is held changes pitch without restarting the envelopes.

glide.definition: A smooth slide in pitch from one note to the next, instead of jumping.

pitch-bend.definition: A controller, usually a wheel or lever, that slides the pitch of all held notes up or down within a set range.

mod-wheel.definition: A wheel on most keyboards that you move by hand. It does nothing until you connect it to a destination.

aftertouch.definition: Pressure you add by pushing harder on a key after it is down. It does nothing until you connect it to a destination.

key-tracking.definition: Making a setting follow the note you play. With filter key tracking, higher notes open the cutoff so they stay as bright as lower ones.

drive.definition: Pushing a signal harder into the filter so it distorts a little. It adds warmth and extra harmonics.

decibel.definition: A unit of loudness. 0 dB is the loudest setting here; every 6 dB lower is about half the amplitude. Minus infinity is silence.

oscillator.definition: A sound source that repeats a wave shape over and over. How fast it repeats sets the pitch, and the shape sets the tone.

filter.definition: A circuit that turns some frequencies down and lets others through, changing the tone.

amp.definition: Short for amplifier: the stage that sets how loud the sound is.

per-voice.definition: Applied separately to each note you play, so every note has its own envelope, filter and LFO position.

retrigger.definition: Restarting something from the beginning each time you press a key, such as an LFO cycle or an envelope.

sample-and-hold.definition: An LFO shape that picks a new random value at each step and holds it until the next. It gives stepped, random changes.

bypass.definition: Passing the signal through a module untouched, as if it were switched off, so you can compare with and without it.

solo.definition: Muting every other source so you can hear just one on its own.

voice-stealing.definition: When all voices are in use and you play another note, the synth cuts off an older note to free a voice.

anti-aliasing.definition: Techniques that stop frequencies above the limit of digital sound folding back as whistles. They keep high notes clean.

oversampling.definition: Running a process at a higher rate for a moment, so it creates fewer unwanted whistles, then bringing it back down. FM and distortion use it.

hard-sync.definition: A second oscillator restarts its cycle every time the first one restarts. The pitch follows the first, but the shape is cut short, giving a sharp, tearing tone when you sweep the second's pitch.

ring-modulation.definition: Multiplying two waves. The result has their sum and difference frequencies instead of the originals, so it sounds clangy and bell-like.

fm.definition: One oscillator, the modulator, bends the pitch of another, the carrier, at audio speed. It creates extra sidebands around the carrier, spaced by the modulator's frequency. Whole-number ratios sound tuned.

unison.definition: Several copies of one oscillator played together, each tuned slightly differently and placed across the stereo field. It sounds thicker and wider.

distortion.definition: Squashing or clipping a wave so it gains new harmonics. More drive gives a grittier sound.

chorus.definition: An effect that mixes the sound with slightly delayed and detuned copies of itself, so it sounds like more than one player.

delay.definition: An effect that repeats the sound after a gap of time, making an echo.

feedback.definition: Sending some of an effect's output back into its input. In a delay, it makes the echoes repeat and fade.

reverb.definition: An effect that adds the dense reflections of a room, so the sound seems to happen in a space. The tail after the note is the reverb.

damping.definition: How quickly high frequencies die away. In reverb, more damping makes a darker, softer tail.

limiter.definition: A safety stage that turns down only the peaks that would go above its ceiling, so the sound does not clip.

tempo-sync.definition: Setting a time or rate as a musical note length, such as 1/4, instead of seconds or Hz, so it follows the tempo.

bpm.definition: Beats per minute: the tempo. In a plugin it comes from your host; standalone it is 120.

ping-pong.definition: A delay that bounces its echoes between the left and right speakers.

wet-dry.definition: The balance between the original sound (dry) and the effect's processed sound (wet). 0% is all dry; 100% is all wet.
